\section[\ml{മണി}]{\ml{മണി} — one word in Malayalam's dictionaries, two in Tamil's}

\label{lesson:ML-C18-mani}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Kannada and Telugu both borrowed Sanskrit's "bell" word for "hour." Malayalam's story is genuinely murkier — and it's about to disagree with its closest cousin, Tamil, on how this exact word is even structured.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\textbf{\ml{മണി}} (\emph{mani}) = "\textbf{hour, o'clock}" — and it also means "\textbf{bell, gong}" and "\textbf{gem, jewel, pearl}." Here's the honest, slightly untidy part: Malayalam's own dictionary tradition treats \textbf{all three of these senses as ONE word}, borrowed from Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{मणि}} (\emph{maṇi}, "gem, jewel, pearl") — the same Sanskrit word behind names like \emph{Manipravalam} and the mantra syllable in "\emph{om mani padme hum}." Under this account, "bell/hour" isn't a separate native word at all — it's just another meaning that grew out of the same borrowed "gem" word (a bell-shaped gem or ornament, perhaps, extending to the bell itself, and then to the hour it announces).

\begin{culture}
Here's what makes this genuinely interesting rather than settled: Tamil's closely related cognate \textbf{\ta{மணி}} is analyzed very differently by Tamil's own reference dictionaries — as \textbf{two separate, unrelated words} that happen to be spelled and pronounced identically: a \textbf{native Dravidian} "bell, gong" word (which extends to "hour"), and a completely separate Sanskrit loan meaning "gem." The broader comparative Dravidian dictionary (DEDR) does list Malayalam among the languages sharing that native "bell" word too — but even DEDR flags a possible Sanskrit connection for the whole word-family as unresolved. So: two closest-cousin languages, and even the specialists don't fully agree on whether this is one Sanskrit word wearing three meanings, or a native word and a Sanskrit word that just happen to sound alike.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: telling the time}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഒരു} \ml{മണി}.} — "One o'clock." (\emph{oru mani}, "one hour/bell") \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}.} — "Two o'clock." (\emph{raṇṭŭ mani}, "two hour/bell")
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "mani" — hour, also "bell," also "gem" — genuinely debated whether that's one word or two{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "oru mani" — one o'clock{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the honest point — Malayalam's own dictionaries call it one Sanskrit word; Tamil's call the bell/hour sense a separate, native word{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} According to Malayalam's own dictionary tradition, are "hour," "bell," and "gem" one word or two? (\textbf{One} — all traced to Sanskrit \emph{maṇi}, "gem.") How does Tamil's own dictionary tradition treat its cognate word differently? (As \textbf{two separate, unrelated homophones} — a native "bell/hour" word and a distinct Sanskrit "gem" loan.) Is this fully settled? (\textbf{No} — even the comparative Dravidian dictionary flags the Sanskrit connection as an open question.)
\end{tcolorbox}
